title: Theory of exciton-exciton interactions in crystalline systems
authors: L. Maisel Licerán, H. T. C. Stoof
abstract: Excitons are bound electron-hole pairs in semiconductors whose interactions influence optical properties and determine their collective behavior and emergent correlated phases. Despite the theoretical and experimental significance of these phenomena, a microscopic theory of exciton-exciton interactions that takes into account the full composite nature of these quasiparticles is lacking. Here, we present a general theory of exciton-exciton interactions that builds upon our previous publication [Physical Review B 113, 155440 (2026)], which applied only to conventional semiconductors with weak band hybridization. By contrast, the theory presented here is valid in virtually any crystalline semiconducting system and can be applied to the study of biexciton formation and correlated excitonic phases in systems where band topology, quantum geometry, and moiré effects play a significant role. In addition to the analytical theory, we also present results in simple systems with flat bands with a nontrivial quantum metric and show that the biexcitonic spectrum differs strongly from that in the case without quantum geometry. Our theory paves the way for accurate quantitative calculations of biexciton spectra and excitonic many-body phases in modern condensed-matter systems.
summary: This paper presents a generalized microscopic theory for exciton-exciton interactions in crystalline semiconductors, moving beyond models restricted to simple materials. It develops the theory from the single-exciton Bethe–Salpeter equation to a full biexciton eigenvalue problem. The resulting framework allows for accurate quantitative predictions of correlated excitonic phases, particularly in systems exhibiting complex band structures like those found in 2D materials.
main_problem: Developing a general microscopic theory for exciton-exciton interactions that accounts for the full composite nature of excitons, applicable beyond conventional semiconductors.
main_result: The theory successfully generalizes previous work to systems with nontrivial quantum geometry, showing that the biexcitonic spectrum strongly depends on these geometric effects.
method: The theory builds upon the Bethe–Salpeter equation (BSE) for single excitons and extends it to a generalized eigenvalue problem for biexcitons, resulting in a Schrödinger-like equation.
model_or_system: The study focuses on exciton-exciton interactions in crystalline semiconducting systems, applicable to 2D materials and those exhibiting band topology or moiré effects.
key_observables: Exciton dispersions, biexciton binding energies, and the biexcitonic spectrum.
important_parameters: Band topology, quantum geometry, and the degree of band hybridization.
main_assumptions: The initial derivation assumes conservation of 'flavors' at the interaction vertex, and the final simplification involves approximations regarding the summation over exciton states.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the general Hamiltonian and the single-exciton BSE to formulating the complex biexciton eigenvalue problem, simplifying it through symmetry arguments, and finally presenting the resulting Schrödinger-like equation for the biexciton energy.
why_interesting: The formalism for handling composite quasiparticles (excitons) and extending the interaction theory to incorporate underlying band structure details (quantum geometry) is highly relevant for understanding strongly correlated phases in modern 2D materials.

The ground-state exciton, shown in blue, has a finite effective mass at the Γ point despite the flatness of the electron and hole bands. The two exciton modes are well separated in energy for 𝛿≳0.1. The grey dashed line marks the electron–hole continuum, which is constant for the flat-band system. The axes are equal in all plots.

The small plots on the side correspond to the position-space probability densities, obtained via Fourier transformation of the momentum- space wave functions. Note that Φ𝑲(𝑹) is defined on the Bravais lattice, so that each square in these plots represents the excitonic weight on one unit cell.
